**Setting up the numbers**

- Prevalence: P(disease) = 1/500 = 0.002, so P(no disease) = 0.998
- Sensitivity: P(test+ | disease) = 0.98
- Specificity: P(test− | no disease) = 0.95, so P(test+ | no disease) = 0.05

**Applying Bayes' theorem**

P(disease | test+) = [P(test+|disease)·P(disease)] / [P(test+|disease)·P(disease) + P(test+|no disease)·P(no disease)]

Numerator: 0.98 × 0.002 = 0.00196
Denominator terms: 0.00196 + (0.05 × 0.998) = 0.00196 + 0.0499 = 0.05186

P(disease | test+) = 0.00196 / 0.05186 ≈ 0.037794 → **3.78%**

**Why this is counterintuitive:** Even with a 98%-sensitive, 95%-specific test, because the condition is rare (0.2% prevalence), the pool of healthy people is so much larger that the 5% false-positive rate among them generates far more false positives (≈49.9 per 1,000 tested) than there are true positives (≈2 per 1,000 tested) — so most positives are false alarms.

FINAL ANSWER: 3.78
